title: Asoka Halwa
story: Many years ago, as a kid, every time we went to our ancestral home in Thiruvarur, I ate Asoka. I still distinctly remember it.

Later, when I was studying engineering in Thanjavur, I found out what a famous sweet Asoka is down there. Every time I visited Thanjavur and Kumbakonam, there it was. Somewhere along the way, Asoka halwa became one of my favorite South Indian sweets.
So here is my Asoka halwa.
ingredients: ½ cup (about 100 g) moong dal (paasi paruppu)
2 tbsp oat flour or almond flour
1 pinch red or orange food color, optional
steps: Wash the moong dal and pressure cook it with about 1½ cups of water, 4 whistles on medium flame, until nice and mushy.
Let it cool a little, then mash it well, or better, grind it smooth in the mixer.
In a pan, melt ¼ cup of the ghee and roast the cashews until golden. Take them out and keep aside.
In the same ghee, roast the oat or almond flour on a low to medium flame for about a minute, until it smells nutty. Almond flour browns fast, so keep an eye on it.
Add the ground dal, mix well, and cook for about 2 minutes.
Once it starts to thicken, add the sugar. It'll loosen up as soon as the sugar goes in, and that's normal. Keep cooking on medium until it thickens again.
Add the rest of the ghee a tablespoon at a time, stirring. It comes together and rolls around the pan without sticking.
If you want the color, mix the pinch in a little water and stir it in until even.
Add the cardamom, the roasted cashews and a last spoon of ghee. Mix, cook a few more minutes, and turn off the flame.
tip: Traditionally Asoka uses wheat flour. I use oat or almond flour instead. It still gives that lovely texture, with a nice nutty note.
closing: That's it. Hot Asoka halwa is ready.

nutrition.yield: Makes about 575 g, so 4 servings of about 145 g (about 570 kcal each). Almond flour comes out practically the same.
